title_full_ar: الموطأ للإمام مالك بن أنس الأصبحي
subject: hadith
summary: Al-Muwatta is the earliest surviving comprehensive Islamic legal text, compiled by Imam Malik ibn Anas al-Asbahi (93–179 AH / 711–795 CE), the founder of the Maliki school of jurisprudence. It combines hadith, the practice of the people of Medina (amal ahl al-Madinah), and Imam Malik's own juridical opinions, and is considered among the most authoritative works in both hadith and Maliki fiqh.
overview:
Imam Malik ibn Anas was born in Medina around 93 AH and died there in 179 AH, spending virtually his entire scholarly life in the city of the Prophet ﷺ. He studied under major scholars of the Successor generation (Tabi'in), including Nafi' (the freedman of Ibn Umar) and Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, giving him direct chains of transmission to Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. Imam al-Shafi'i, Imam Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani, and many other major scholars studied under Imam Malik.

Al-Muwatta — the title means 'the well-trodden path' or 'the levelled way' — was compiled over a period of decades and reportedly went through several recensions as Imam Malik continually refined and reduced the narrations. According to some accounts, the original contained tens of thousands of narrations and was progressively reduced to its present form. The work integrates three types of material: prophetic hadith (marfu'), narrations from the Companions (mawquf), and statements from the Successors (maqtu'), along with Imam Malik's own legal opinions and his invocations of ijma' (consensus) and amal (the practice of Medina's scholars).

The concept of amal ahl al-Madinah — the lived practice of Medina's scholars as a source of legal authority — is central to Maliki jurisprudence and is woven throughout al-Muwatta. Imam Malik held that the practice of the scholars of Medina, who had inherited the Prophet's ﷺ city and his Companions' legacy, carried strong evidential weight, in some cases outweighing isolated hadith chains.

Al-Muwatta survives in multiple transmissions (riwayat) by different students of Imam Malik, the most significant being the riwayah of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Masmudi al-Andalusi, which became dominant in North Africa and Andalusia and is the basis of most printed editions. Other important transmissions include those of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani (the Hanafi jurist, who transmitted his own riwayah with comparisons to Hanafi positions), al-Shafi'i, and Abu Mus'ab al-Zuhri.

The work is organised in the standard fiqhi order, covering purity, prayer, zakah, fasting, pilgrimage, business, marriage, criminal law, and many other topics. It contains approximately 1,720 hadith in Yahya's riwayah, along with numerous statements of Companions and Successors. Due to its early compilation and Imam Malik's exceptionally high standards for the narrators he accepted, the hadith in al-Muwatta are generally considered among the most reliable in all hadith literature, with Imam al-Shafi'i reportedly saying, 'There is no book on earth after the Qur'an more sound than Malik's book.'

Major commentaries include al-Tamhid by Imam Ibn Abd al-Barr al-Andalusi (d. 463 AH), considered one of the greatest works of hadith scholarship ever written; al-Istidhkar, also by Ibn Abd al-Barr; and al-Masalik fi Sharh Muwatta' Malik by Ibn al-Arabi al-Maliki (d. 543 AH). Modern commentary includes Tanwir al-Hawalik by Imam al-Suyuti (d. 911 AH).

The standard English translation is by Aisha Abdurrahman Bewley (Diwan Press / Madinah Press), based on Yahya's riwayah. A translation of the Shaybani riwayah with comparative Hanafi commentary has been published by the Islamic Book Trust (Kuala Lumpur). A newer English translation by Mohammed Fadel and Connell Monette (Harvard University Press, 2019) provides a fresh scholarly rendering with extensive annotation.

The Muwatta's historical influence across the Islamic world is difficult to overstate. It was the first Islamic scholarly text to achieve wide geographical distribution across the major centres of the Muslim world in Imam Malik's own lifetime and shortly after his death. The Maliki school, which spread from Medina through North Africa, Andalusia, and sub-Saharan Africa largely on the authority of al-Muwatta's transmission chains, has governed the fiqh of hundreds of millions of Muslims for over twelve centuries. The Muwatta was also foundational to al-Bukhari's methodology: many of the chains in Sahih al-Bukhari pass through narrators whose transmission Malik validated. Imam al-Shafi'i, after studying under Imam Malik for years, carried the Muwatta back to Egypt and Iraq as a primary source. It is available in full on sunnah.com.
structure: 61 books (kutub), approximately 1,720 hadith (Yahya's riwayah), plus statements of Companions and Successors
